query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, earlier studies separately examined tensile creep at 1250 °C, microhardness changes during cold rolling, elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K, and hardening after aging at 600–800 °C. However, these findings do not provide a unified explanation of the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior. Thermal expansion is also relevant because mismatch can produce thermal stresses during composite solidification and potentially affect strength. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the unresolved behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, observations predicted relative to a baseline, the relevant temperature and response boundaries, how the earlier findings support the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The apparent discrepancies in stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior of the HfNbTaTiZr alloy arise because temperature‐dependent amplification of internal residual stresses—generated by differential thermal expansion at sub‐grain interfaces formed during cold rolling and aging—modulates the dislocation network and lattice distortion. This results in unified changes in creep rate, hardness, and elastic moduli across the temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single-phase BCC HfNbTaTiZr refractory high‐entropy alloy in its as-cast state, with subsequent processing (cold rolling and/or aging) to introduce dislocation networks and nano-scale phase features.
generation.intervention: Prepare two sets of samples: one that is heavily cold rolled (to induce high dislocation density and stress-induced phase transformation) and one that is solution annealed to minimize processing-induced defects. Subject both sets to controlled thermal cycling or tests spanning room temperature up to 1250 °C.
generation.conditions: Tensile testing, creep experiments, and elastic modulus measurements performed over discrete temperature intervals (e.g., RT, 600–800 °C, and near 1250 °C) along with dilatometry to assess thermal expansion. The tests should be executed at strain rates and loading conditions relevant for tensile creep and hardness evaluation.
generation.structural_mediator: The internal dislocation density and sub-grain boundary lattice distortions that develop during cold rolling and age-induced precipitation, which are further modified by thermal expansion mismatch at these microstructural interfaces.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the inherent high thermal expansion coefficient of the alloy leads to increased differential strain between sub-grains and interfaces. In samples with high dislocation densities from cold rolling or aging, this mismatch intensifies internal residual stresses that enhance dislocation pinning and alter lattice stiffness. Consequently, yield strength, creep resistance, and the overall elastic moduli become strongly temperature dependent and unified under this mechanism.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the solution-annealed baseline, cold-rolled and aged samples will show higher hardness and yield strength at room temperature that are more resistant to thermal softening at elevated temperatures due to the persistence of internal residual stresses. Temperature-dependent dilatometry will reveal increased effective thermal expansion (indicative of local mismatch strains) in cold-worked samples, correlating with modified elastic moduli and creep behavior.
generation.baseline: HfNbTaTiZr alloy samples processed by solution annealing, which exhibit minimal dislocation-induced lattice distortions and lower internal residual stresses.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to be operative over a wide temperature range (293 K to approximately 1250 °C) and becomes especially pronounced in conditions where the dislocation density is high (e.g., cold-rolled or lightly aged states) compared to well-recrystallized (strain-free) microstructures.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative contributions of dislocation density versus thermal expansion-induced lattice mismatch remain uncertain; further atomic-scale and thermomechanical modeling are required to separate these effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of HfNbTaTiZr samples: one group processed by heavy cold rolling to obtain a high dislocation density and sub-grain boundary structure and another group processed by solution annealing to eliminate these defects. Further modify a subset of each group by minor alloying to adjust the intrinsic thermal expansion coefficient. Conduct tensile, creep, and elastic modulus tests over the temperature range from 293 K to 1250 °C, and perform dilatometric measurements to monitor thermal expansion behavior and evaluate internal stress evolution.
measurements: Elastic moduli (via resonance ultrasound spectroscopy or in situ XRD)
Yield strength and creep behavior (via high-temperature tensile tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If variations in dislocation density or modifications to the thermal expansion coefficient do not result in corresponding changes in yield strength, creep resistance, or elastic moduli, or if both cold-rolled and annealed samples exhibit the same thermoelastic behavior regardless of their internal residual stresses, then the hypothesis that thermal expansion–induced internal stresses are governing the unified behavior will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Overall, this comprehensive study provides evidence for the unique elastic and plastic deformation behavior of the single BCC solid-solution phase refractory HEA at elevated temperatures using in situ neutron experiments coupled with theoretical calculations. The results of the ND and characterization of the microstructure show the excellent BCC single-phase stability up to 900°C. Furthermore, the present alloy has the high yield strength and excellent plasticity at RT and softening resistance at elevated temperatures. The lattice strain evolution results show the distinctive elastic deformation behavior as an elastic isotropy at RT and less temperature dependency in the elastic anisotropic deformation behavior than conventional metallic materials at elevated temperatures. The single-crystal elastic moduli are obtained from the in situ ND data coupled with the Kroner model approach, showing excellent agreement with the experimental values determined from RUS measurements and first-principles calculations.
